# Q5: In a paragraph, summarise your findings and suggest directions for future research.

Our research into Parkinson's disease (PD) brought together four study arms — population genetics, RNA-seq, drug screening and a clinical trial — to investigate the genetic, molecular and clinical factors associated with PD. Population genetics analysis found significantly higher polygenic risk scores (PRS) in PD patients than healthy controls, although substantial overlap between groups suggests that PRS alone is not a reliable predictor of disease status. RNA-seq analysis identified 30 differentially expressed genes associated with dopamine biosynthesis and oxidative stress responses, highlighting pathways that may be involved in PD pathology. Drug screening identified four compounds associated with increased neuronal viability following MPP exposure, three of which targeted genes (MOXD1, SULT1A1 and MAOA) that were also upregulated in PD patients. This overlap suggests a possible relationship between dopamine regulation and neuronal survival, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In the clinical trial, the new compound and exercise were associated with improved gait, while older patients generally demonstrated poorer balance. Although no significant relationship was found between PRS and gait overall, a treatment-specific association suggests that genetic risk may influence treatment response. Despite these findings, small sample sizes, limited genetic coverage and incomplete donor information restricted our ability to draw broader conclusions across the four study arms. Future research should investigate these relationships in larger patient cohorts, validate the effects and mechanisms of the identified compounds, and explore whether genetic and molecular characteristics can help predict treatment outcomes. Together, these approaches could improve our understanding of PD and guide the development of more effective treatments.
